core.text: To say *when* something happens, Latin uses a bare ablative with no preposition: **the ablative (the 'at / in (a time)' form)**. *Nocte sōl nōn lūcet* — at night the sun does not shine; *hōrā sextā* — at the sixth hour; *mēnse Iūniō* — in June; *eō tempore* — at that time; *hieme, aestāte, vēre* — in winter, in summer, in spring. The time word simply takes its ablative ending, and English supplies *at, in* or *on*. Latin name: ablātīvus temporis.
English needs a preposition for time — *at night, in June, on Monday*. Latin drops it and lets the ending do the work, just as it drops *with* in *gladiō pugnat* (fights with a sword).
A time word in the ablative, without a preposition, answers 'when?'

invented.en: In winter the boys stay at home.

core.text: The same case says where and when. *In hortō* (in the garden) keeps *in*; *nocte* (at night) has nothing. Place usually keeps the preposition, time usually drops it. So a bare ablative of a time word — *nocte, diē, hōrā, annō, mēnse, tempore, hieme* — is time; a bare ablative of a place word is rare in prose (towns and *domī* apart).

teach.title: What it does
teach.say: English needs a little word for time — *at* night, *in* winter, *on* that day. Latin does not: it puts the time word into **the ablative (the 'at / in (a time)' form)** and leaves it bare. *Nocte* on its own means 'at night'; *hieme* means 'in winter'. The ending does the work the English preposition does.

check.ask: Which word says when, and which little English word does its ending do the work of?

teach.title: The ending on a 1st- or 2nd-declension time word
teach.say: One cell. A time word of the 1st declension takes the ablative singular *-ā*, marked with a long vowel: *hōra* → *hōrā*, at the hour. A 2nd-declension one takes *-ō* in just the same way: *annus* → *annō*, in the year; *autumnus* → *autumnō*, in autumn. When the time word brings an adjective with it — *hōrā prīmā*, at the first hour — that word takes the ablative too; step 4 comes back to it.

show.say: hōrā — the short -a of hōra becomes a long -ā

check.ask: ___ prīmā lūx in caelō est. At the first hour — a 1st-declension time word takes the long *-ā*. (hōra)

teach.title: The 3rd declension -e and the 5th -ē
teach.say: Most of the book's time words are 3rd declension, and their ablative singular is a short *-e*: *nocte*, *vespere*, *tempore*, *mēnse*, *aestāte*, *hieme*. The 5th declension has a long *-ē*: *diē*, *merīdiē*.

show.say: aestāte — the 3rd declension takes a short -e

check.ask: ___ familia in ātriō sedet. In the evening — the 3rd declension takes a short *-e*. (vesper)

teach.title: An adjective with it goes into the ablative too
teach.say: Time phrases usually come in two words, and both take the ablative ending: *hōrā prīmā* (at the first hour), *eō tempore* (at that time), *illō diē* (on that day), *mēnse Iānuāriō* (in the month of January), *aestāte calidā* (in the warm summer).

check.ask: *Illō diē* is two words. What case is each one in, and why must they match?

teach.title: Telling it from the ablative of place
teach.say: The same case says *where* and *when*, so use the preposition as your signpost. Place keeps *in*: *in cubiculō*, in the bedroom. Time drops it: *nocte*, at night. In *Nocte Iūlius in cubiculō dormit* both are there — the bare word is the time, the one after *in* is the place.

check.ask: *Vēre* and *hortō* are both ablative. Which is the time and which is the place, and what tells you?

teach.title: Using it: put the time word in the ablative
teach.say: To say when, take the time word, put it in the ablative, and add no preposition at all: *annus* → *illō annō*, in that year; *diēs* → *diē*, by day. If you find yourself reaching for *in*, you are thinking in English.

check.ask: Nocte et ___ flūmen fluit. By night and by day — and no preposition at all. (diēs)

more.text: How long something lasts is the accusative (the object form), not the ablative: *trēs hōrās dormit* — he sleeps for three hours; *multōs annōs* — for many years. Within how long is the ablative again: *tribus diēbus* — within three days. *Paucīs diēbus* can mean either 'within' or 'a few days later' by context.

The learner's notes (week 13): a fourth use of the ablative after place, origin and means, answering *when?* or *at what time?*; Classical Latin has no preposition (*nocte hominēs dormiunt*, *diē hominēs operantur*), but medieval Latin often writes *in autumnō*, *sub nocte*. Use the classical way in composition; expect *in* in later readings.

Ørberg (chapter XIII) uses it throughout the calendar chapter: *mēnse Iūniō diēs longī sunt*, *diēbus prīmīs mēnsium*, *hōrā sextā vel merīdiē*, *nocte*. A&G §423: set phrases behave the same — *initiō* (at the beginning), *fīne* (at the end), *tempore* (in time), *bellō* (in the war).
